title: 0770 The Impact of Acute Sleep Extension on Blood Pressure Is Dependent on Sleep Quality

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title> <jats:p>About 30% of the U.S. population sleep less than 7-hours per night, with this proportion of adults having a greater prevalence of hypertension than adults that meet the recommended amount of sleep. Middle-aged to older adults are of particular interest as they have lower sleep durations than younger adults, and suffer from higher rates of cardiovascular disease. Therefore, more research is needed in this population to understand the impact of sleep duration on vascular health. The aim of this study was to determine the impact of one night of sleep extension on blood pressure and microvascular function in middle-aged to older adults.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Methods</jats:title> <jats:p>Sleep and daily physical activity were objectively measured at home for two weeks using wrist actigraphy in 22 adults (60 ± 15y). Vascular measurements were made in the morning on the 8th and 15th day. Participants spent at least 10h in bed on the night prior to one of these testing days to extend sleep. Mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) and peak reactive hyperemia in the forearm were measured on each testing day.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Results</jats:title> <jats:p>Reactive hyperemia and MAP were unaltered (P>0.05) by sleep extension in the total sample. However, adults that experienced improved sleep efficiency during extended sleep (n=10, 4.2 ± 1.4%) exhibited reduced MAP (-5.5 ± 4.6 mm Hg, P=0.005) while adults that had little change or decreased sleep efficiency (n=12, -1.7 ± 2.9%) showed no change in MAP. The reduction in MAP was significantly different between sleep efficiency groups (P=0.005, Hedges’ g = 1.21) after adjustment for sex and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title> <jats:p>These results suggest that one night of sleep extension has the potential to reduce blood pressure in midlife to older adults when the additional sleep time improves quality of sleep.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Support (if any)</jats:title> <jats:p>This study was funded by the American Heart Association (19IPLOI34760579; J.U. Gonzales).</jats:p> </jats:sec>
